waffen-grundlagen-01.question: What is the primary purpose of the German Weapons Act (WaffG)?

options.a: It exclusively regulates commercial trade in sporting firearms.
options.b: It regulates dealing with weapons or ammunition, taking public safety and order into account.
options.c: It exclusively regulates the training of hunters.
options.d: It only regulates the export of weapons abroad.

waffen-grundlagen-01.explanation: Under Sec. 1(1) WaffG, the Act governs dealing with weapons or ammunition with regard to public safety and order. It is primarily safety/public-order law, not commercial law.

waffen-grundlagen-02.question: Which of the following is NOT covered by the legal concept of "dealing with" (Umgang) a weapon under German law?

options.a: Acquiring a firearm.
options.b: Carrying a weapon outside one's own home.
options.c: Merely looking at a weapon displayed in a case without any physical interaction.
options.d: Transporting a weapon across a border.

waffen-grundlagen-02.explanation: Under Sec. 1(3) WaffG, "dealing with" a weapon or ammunition covers acquiring, possessing, transferring, carrying, transporting, taking along, firing, manufacturing, working on, repairing, or trading it. Merely looking at a weapon without possession or physical interaction is not legally "dealing with" it.

waffen-grundlagen-03.question: How is a "firearm" (Schusswaffe) essentially defined under German weapons law?

options.a: An object designed, among other things, for attack, defense, hunting, or sport, in which projectiles are propelled through a barrel.
options.b: Any object that can fire a projectile without a barrel.
options.c: Only fully automatic weapons.
options.d: Only objects used by the police.

waffen-grundlagen-03.explanation: Under Annex 1, Section 1, Subsection 1, No. 1.1 WaffG, firearms are objects intended for attack, defense, signaling, hunting, distance injection, marking, sport, or play, in which projectiles are propelled through a barrel.

waffen-grundlagen-04.question: From what age is dealing with weapons or ammunition generally permitted in Germany?

options.a: From age 16, with parental consent.
options.b: Only from the completed age of 18.
options.c: From age 21 without exception.
options.d: There is no general age limit.

waffen-grundlagen-04.explanation: Under Sec. 2(1) WaffG, dealing with weapons or ammunition is generally only permitted for persons who have reached the age of 18. Specific supervised exceptions (e.g., shooting sport under supervision) exist but do not change this baseline rule.

waffen-grundlagen-05.question: Which statement about the permit-requirement/prohibition system under the WaffG is correct?

options.a: All weapons are permit-free unless expressly prohibited.
options.b: All weapons are subject to a blanket prohibition without exception.
options.c: Weapons listed in Annex 2 Section 2 require a permit; weapons listed in Annex 2 Section 1 are generally prohibited.
options.d: The permit requirement and prohibition apply only to ammunition, never to firearms.

waffen-grundlagen-05.explanation: Under Sec. 2(2) WaffG, dealing with weapons/ammunition listed in Annex 2 Section 2 requires a permit; under Sec. 2(3) WaffG, dealing with items listed in Annex 2 Section 1 is prohibited. Exemptions from both the permit requirement and the prohibition also exist (Annex 2 Sections 1 and 2).

waffen-grundlagen-06.question: What is the Sachkunde (expertise) certificate under Sec. 7 WaffG typically required for?

options.a: Exclusively for a private individual's purchase of a single hunting rifle.
options.b: Among other things, for certain weapons-related professional activities such as the security-guard sector, and for certain hunting/sport-shooting contexts where weapons law requires it.
options.c: For every retail purchase of ammunition, regardless of weapon type.
options.d: Only for weapons collectors owning more than 50 firearms.

waffen-grundlagen-06.explanation: The Sec. 7 WaffG expertise certificate demonstrates technical and legal weapons knowledge. It is required, among other things, for certain commercial/professional contexts such as the security-guard sector and for certain hunting/sport-shooting situations where weapons law demands it — it is not a general prerequisite for every single ammunition purchase.

waffen-grundlagen-07.question: How can the Sachkunde certificate generally be obtained under Sec. 7(1) WaffG?

options.a: By passing an examination before the designated authority, or by otherwise demonstrating expertise through relevant activity or training.
options.b: Only through at least ten years of shooting-club membership.
options.c: Only through a university law degree.
options.d: The law does not actually provide for any such proof.

waffen-grundlagen-07.explanation: Under Sec. 7(1) WaffG, proof of expertise is furnished by passing an examination before the designated body, or by otherwise demonstrating expertise through relevant activity or training (further detailed in the AWaffV).

waffen-grundlagen-08.question: What distinguishes a semi-automatic firearm from a fully automatic firearm?

options.a: A semi-automatic weapon can fire multiple shots from a single pull of the trigger.
options.b: A semi-automatic weapon reloads itself automatically after each shot, but only one shot is fired per trigger pull.
options.c: Semi-automatic weapons generally have no magazine.
options.d: There is no legally relevant distinction between the two weapon types.

waffen-grundlagen-08.explanation: Under the systematics of German weapons law, semi-automatic firearms automatically become ready to fire again after a shot is discharged, but each individual pull of the trigger releases only one further shot — unlike a fully automatic weapon, where a single trigger pull can release multiple shots.

waffen-grundlagen-09.question: What generally distinguishes a "short weapon" (e.g., pistol or revolver) from a "long weapon" under German weapons law?

options.a: Threshold values for barrel length and/or the overall length of the weapon.
options.b: The caliber of the ammunition used.
options.c: The color of the grip.
options.d: The number of rounds the magazine holds.

waffen-grundlagen-09.explanation: Under weapons law, short weapons are distinguished by length thresholds: the barrel and closed action together must be shorter than a defined length, and/or the shortest intended overall length must not exceed a defined value. Caliber alone is not decisive for this classification.

waffen-grundlagen-10.question: Which statement about so-called "soft-air" (airsoft-type) weapons is correct under German weapons law?

options.a: Soft-air weapons can never be classified as a weapon under the Weapons Act.
options.b: Soft-air weapons are never subject to the Weapons Act, regardless of projectile energy.
options.c: Soft-air devices that propel a projectile through a barrel are already classified as firearms; if the projectile energy stays at or below 7.5 joules and the device bears the official test mark, acquisition and possession are exempt from the permit requirement — above that threshold, or without the mark, the standard permit requirement applies.
options.d: Soft-air weapons are purely toys and are therefore always excluded from the scope of the Weapons Act.

waffen-grundlagen-10.explanation: Soft-air devices that use a spring, gas, or similar propulsion to drive a projectile through a barrel already meet the general definition of a firearm (Annex 1, Section 1, Subsection 1, No. 1.1 WaffG). If their projectile energy stays at or below 7.5 joules and they bear the official test mark (F in a pentagon), acquisition and possession are exempt from the permit requirement under Annex 2, Section 2, Subsection 2, No. 1.1 WaffG; above that threshold, or without the mark, the standard permit requirement applies (Sec. 24(2) WaffG). Soft-air weapons are therefore neither generally permit-free nor mere toys outside the scope of weapons law.

waffen-grundlagen-11.question: What happens if there is doubt whether a particular object falls within the scope of the Weapons Act?

options.a: The owner has final, independent authority to decide the classification.
options.b: Upon application, the competent authority decides on the classification; certain persons and authorities are entitled to apply.
options.c: In such cases, the object is automatically treated as out of scope.
options.d: Only a court can decide the classification, and only at first instance.

waffen-grundlagen-11.explanation: Under Sec. 2(5) WaffG, if there is doubt about how to classify an object, the competent authority decides upon application; those entitled to apply include manufacturers, importers, acquirers, or possessors with a legitimate interest, as well as competent federal and state authorities. The decision is generally binding within the Act's scope.

waffen-grundlagen-12.question: Who generally bears responsibility under the Weapons Act for preventing a weapon from being lost or taken by an unauthorized third party?

options.a: Whoever possesses the weapon or ammunition.
options.b: Exclusively the local police authority.
options.c: Exclusively the weapon's manufacturer.
options.d: No one — the risk lies solely with an insurer.

waffen-grundlagen-12.explanation: Under Sec. 36(1) WaffG, whoever possesses weapons or ammunition must take the necessary precautions to prevent them from being lost or taken by unauthorized third parties. This duty rests personally on the possessor.

waffen-grundlagen-13.question: Do cutting and thrusting weapons (e.g., certain knives) also count as "weapons" under German weapons law?

options.a: No, the Weapons Act covers firearms only.
options.b: No, such objects are governed exclusively by the Criminal Code.
options.c: Yes, portable objects that by their nature are designed to eliminate or reduce a person's capacity to attack or defend, such as cutting and thrusting weapons, also count as weapons.
options.d: Yes, but only if they are made of metal.

waffen-grundlagen-13.explanation: Under Sec. 1(2) No. 2 WaffG, "weapons" include not only firearms but also portable objects that by their nature are designed to eliminate or reduce a person's capacity to attack or defend, in particular cutting and thrusting weapons. The WaffG's concept of "weapon" is thus broader than firearms alone.

waffen-munition-01.question: What components typically make up a complete centerfire cartridge?

options.a: Only a projectile and propellant powder, without a case.
options.b: Case, primer, propellant powder, and projectile.
options.c: Only a case with a primer, without a projectile.
options.d: Only shot pellets, without a case.

waffen-munition-01.explanation: A cartridge for centerfire weapons typically consists of the case, the primer, the propellant powder, and the projectile. All four components work together functionally when the shot is fired.

waffen-munition-02.question: What is generally meant by the "caliber" of ammunition/a weapon?

options.a: A measurement or designation that essentially characterizes the diameter of the projectile or bore.
options.b: The maximum number of cartridges a magazine can hold.
options.c: The overall length of the finished cartridge in centimeters.
options.d: The weight of the weapon without ammunition.

waffen-munition-02.explanation: Caliber is a measurement/designation that essentially describes the diameter of the projectile or the bore of the barrel (e.g., 9 mm, .357). It is a key technical distinguishing feature of ammunition and weapons.

waffen-munition-03.question: Why is so-called hollow-point (expanding) ammunition subject to special rules under weapons law?

options.a: Because it is exclusively permitted in competitive sport shooting.
options.b: Because on impact it deforms/expands more than full metal jacket projectiles, producing a different terminal effect, which is why special restrictions on dealing with it apply.
options.c: Because it is generally lighter than other projectiles.
options.d: Because it is exclusively intended for export.

waffen-munition-03.explanation: Hollow-point/expanding projectiles deform and expand more on impact than shape-stable full metal jacket projectiles, producing a different terminal effect. This distinct effect is the reason for separate, more restrictive legal rules governing this ammunition.

waffen-munition-04.question: What generally distinguishes single-projectile (ball) ammunition from shot (buckshot/birdshot) ammunition?

options.a: Ball ammunition is fired exclusively from shotguns, shot ammunition exclusively from rifles.
options.b: There is no technical difference, only the name differs.
options.c: Ball ammunition contains a single, shaped projectile, while shot ammunition contains many small pellets that spread out after leaving the barrel.
options.d: Shot ammunition generally contains no propellant powder.

waffen-munition-04.explanation: Ball ammunition fires a single shaped projectile (typical for rifles), while shot ammunition contains a number of small pellets that spread out after leaving the barrel (typical for shotguns).

waffen-munition-05.question: Which statement about the legal classification of ammunition is generally correct?

options.a: Ammunition is never subject to its own storage rules; only the weapon itself is.
options.b: Ammunition subject to a permit requirement is, like permit-required firearms, independently covered by weapons-law storage requirements.
options.c: Ammunition may generally be stored freely accessible next to the weapon.
options.d: Only the Explosives Act governs ammunition.

waffen-munition-05.explanation: Ammunition whose acquisition is not exempt from the permit requirement is subject to its own security requirements (among others under Sec. 13 AWaffV), independent of the requirements applicable to the associated firearm. Freely accessible joint storage is specifically not the default rule.

waffen-munition-06.question: How are the three classic sub-fields of ballistics generally distinguished?

options.a: Interior ballistics (processes inside the barrel), exterior ballistics (the projectile's flight to the target), and terminal ballistics (effect on the target).
options.b: Only between "live" and "blank" ammunition.
options.c: By the color of the projectiles.
options.d: By the ammunition's country of manufacture.

waffen-munition-06.explanation: Ballistics is classically divided into interior ballistics (processes between ignition and the projectile leaving the barrel), exterior ballistics (the projectile's flight path to the target), and terminal ballistics (the projectile's effect on the target).

waffen-munition-07.question: What effect does air resistance generally have on a projectile's trajectory?

options.a: It further accelerates the projectile after it leaves the barrel.
options.b: It has no effect at all on velocity or trajectory.
options.c: It decelerates the projectile and, together with gravity, produces a curved trajectory.
options.d: It only acts sideways, never in the direction of flight.

waffen-munition-07.explanation: After leaving the barrel, a projectile is decelerated by air resistance; combined with gravity, this produces a curved (roughly parabolic) trajectory rather than a straight line.

waffen-munition-08.question: Why is the "choke" of a shotgun technically relevant?

options.a: It refers to the locking mechanism of the action during reloading.
options.b: It refers to a constriction of the barrel near the muzzle that influences how the shot pattern spreads.
options.c: It refers exclusively to the shotgun's sights.
options.d: It describes a revolver's cylinder capacity.

waffen-munition-08.explanation: The choke is a constriction near the muzzle end of a shotgun barrel. It affects how much the shot pellets spread after leaving the barrel and is therefore relevant to controlling the spread pattern at distance, which has safety implications.

waffen-munition-09.question: What is meant by "caseless ammunition"?

options.a: Ammunition in which the propellant is compressed and bonded directly to the projectile without a conventional metal case.
options.b: Ammunition without any projectile at all.
options.c: Ammunition made entirely of plastic.
options.d: Another term for shot/buckshot ammunition.

waffen-munition-09.explanation: Caseless ammunition dispenses with the conventional metal case; the propellant is instead compressed together with the projectile into a solid block. German weapons law lists it as a separate ammunition category alongside cartridge and pyrotechnic ammunition.

waffen-munition-10.question: Do individual diabolo pellets (round-headed air-rifle pellets without their own propellant/ignition) count as "ammunition" under German weapons law?

options.a: Yes, always, regardless of design.
options.b: Diabolo pellets without their own propellant/primer are generally not "ammunition" under weapons law because they lack the components that characterize ammunition.
options.c: Yes, because they are made of metal.
options.d: No, because they are too light.

waffen-munition-10.explanation: "Ammunition" under weapons law typically requires the interaction of a propellant/primer and a projectile. Diabolo pellets for air guns contain no propellant or primer themselves — the weapon supplies the energy (e.g., via spring pressure or gas) — so they are generally not classified as ammunition under weapons law.

waffen-munition-11.question: Which statement about a firearm's recoil is correct?

options.a: Recoil only occurs with short weapons, never with long weapons.
options.b: Recoil has no bearing on control of the weapon.
options.c: Recoil is the physical reaction force to accelerating the projectile and propellant gases, and must be accounted for in safely holding and handling the weapon.
options.d: Recoil only occurs with defectively manufactured ammunition.

waffen-munition-11.explanation: Under the recoil principle (action = reaction), accelerating the projectile and propellant gases produces an equal and opposite reaction force on the weapon. This recoil must be accounted for safety-consciously when shouldering, holding, and handling the weapon, among other things to avoid losing control of it.

waffen-munition-12.question: Why is it important, as part of the required expertise, to know the approximate range and penetration capability of the ammunition used?

options.a: Because projectiles can continue traveling after missing the intended target or can penetrate obstacles, thereby endangering third parties.
options.b: Because this has no practical consequences for safe handling at all.
options.c: Because this only matters for the ammunition trade.
options.d: Because range is identical across all calibers.

waffen-munition-12.explanation: Depending on caliber, velocity, and the target environment, projectiles can travel much farther or penetrate obstacles more than the immediate target distance might suggest. This knowledge is part of the required expertise and is essential for safely choosing the direction of fire and an adequate backstop.

waffen-aufbewahrung-01.question: What general basic duty does Sec. 36(1) WaffG impose on possessors of weapons and ammunition?

options.a: The duty to take the necessary precautions to prevent weapons or ammunition from being lost or taken by unauthorized third parties.
options.b: The duty to submit weapons to the manufacturer for inspection annually.
options.c: The duty to list every weapon for sale online if unused for a year.
options.d: The duty to store weapons only outside one's own home.

waffen-aufbewahrung-01.explanation: Sec. 36(1) WaffG sets out the basic duty: whoever possesses weapons or ammunition must take the necessary precautions to prevent these items from being lost or taken by unauthorized third parties. The concrete technical requirements are set out in the AWaffV.

waffen-aufbewahrung-02.question: What baseline standard must a security container for permit-required short weapons generally meet under the current AWaffV?

options.a: Any lockable piece of household furniture is sufficient.
options.b: It must meet at least the DIN/EN 1143-1 standard at a defined resistance grade and hold appropriate certification (subject to permissible alternatives / transitional rules for pre-existing containers).
options.c: A simple padlock on a door is always sufficient.
options.d: There is no container requirement at all as long as the weapon is unloaded.

waffen-aufbewahrung-02.explanation: Under Sec. 13(1) AWaffV, permit-required firearms must generally be stored unloaded in a container that meets at least the DIN/EN 1143-1 standard at the defined resistance grade and is certified. Special transitional rules apply to containers lawfully in use before 6 July 2017 (including under the older VDMA 24992 system).

waffen-aufbewahrung-03.question: At minimum, how must permit-required ammunition be stored if it is not already kept together with the weapon in an appropriately certified security container?

options.a: Freely accessible in a drawer.
options.b: In an unlocked cardboard box in the basement.
options.c: At minimum in a sheet-steel container with a pivoting-bolt lock or an equivalent locking device.
options.d: There are no minimum requirements for ammunition at all.

waffen-aufbewahrung-03.explanation: Under Sec. 13(2) No. 2 AWaffV, ammunition whose acquisition is not exempt from the permit requirement must be stored, at minimum, in an unclassified sheet-steel container with a pivoting-bolt lock or an equivalent locking device or an equivalent container.

waffen-aufbewahrung-04.question: May the competent authority enter a permit holder's residential rooms against their will to check on storage compliance?

options.a: Yes, at any time without any particular cause.
options.b: Only to avert imminent dangers to public safety, since to that extent the fundamental right to inviolability of the home is restricted.
options.c: No, entering residential rooms is never permissible under any circumstances.
options.d: Yes, but only between 8 and 10 a.m.

waffen-aufbewahrung-04.explanation: Under Sec. 36(3), sentence 3 WaffG, residential rooms may only be entered against the occupant's will to avert imminent dangers to public safety; the fundamental right to inviolability of the home (Art. 13 Basic Law) is restricted to that extent. There is no unconditional right of entry at any time.

waffen-aufbewahrung-05.question: Are possessors of permit-required weapons obliged to demonstrate to the authority what safekeeping measures they have taken?

options.a: No, no such duty to provide proof generally exists.
options.b: Yes, possessors of permit-required firearms, ammunition, or prohibited weapons must demonstrate to the competent authority the measures taken or planned for secure storage.
options.c: Only if more than 20 weapons are owned.
options.d: Only for weapons dealers, never for private individuals.

waffen-aufbewahrung-05.explanation: Under Sec. 36(3), sentence 1 WaffG, possessors of permit-required firearms, ammunition, or prohibited weapons must demonstrate to the competent authority the measures taken or planned for secure storage. This is a general duty to inform/prove, not a special duty triggered only by owning a large quantity.

waffen-aufbewahrung-06.question: What consequence can improper storage of permit-required weapons or ammunition entail, among other things?

options.a: Only an informal verbal warning with no further consequences.
options.b: Automatic and immediate loss of citizenship.
options.c: Among other things, loss of the required weapons-law reliability, with consequences for existing permits; depending on severity it may also constitute a regulatory offense or even a criminal offense.
options.d: No legal consequences at all as long as no harm has occurred.

waffen-aufbewahrung-06.explanation: Improper storage can, among other things, lead to loss of the reliability required under weapons law, affecting existing permits. Depending on the nature and severity of the violation, it may also constitute a regulatory offense or, in more serious cases, a criminal offense.

waffen-aufbewahrung-07.question: May several authorized persons living in the same household share a single security container for their respective permit-required weapons?

options.a: Yes, joint storage by authorized persons living in the same household is permissible under the statutory conditions.
options.b: No, each person mandatorily needs their own, physically separate container.
options.c: No, joint storage is generally a criminal offense.
options.d: Only if all persons involved own the same type of weapon.

waffen-aufbewahrung-07.explanation: Under certain conditions, weapons law permits joint storage of weapons or ammunition by authorized persons living in the same household — for instance in a shared security container in a family home — provided the other container requirements are met.

waffen-aufbewahrung-08.question: How should permit-required weapons and ammunition generally be secured away from one's own home, e.g., during a hotel stay for a competition?

options.a: Hiding them under the bed without any container is sufficient.
options.b: In this situation, there is no longer any duty to secure them.
options.c: By keeping them under appropriate supervision or through other necessary precautions against loss or unauthorized taking, e.g. a suitable locked container, when the regular storage arrangements are not available on site.
options.d: The weapon must always be carried on one's own body at all times.

waffen-aufbewahrung-08.explanation: For temporary storage away from home, such as in connection with sport shooting, Sec. 13(9) AWaffV governs the matter: if the regular storage required under Sec. 13(1) or (2) AWaffV is not possible, the weapons or ammunition must be kept under appropriate supervision, or secured through other necessary precautions against loss or unauthorized taking — for example, a locked transport container. Hiding them without any security, having no duty to secure them at all, or a strict requirement to always carry the weapon on one's body do not meet this standard.

waffen-aufbewahrung-09.question: How should weapons and ammunition be secured when transported in a vehicle that is briefly left unattended (e.g., while refueling or on a break)?

options.a: They may be left visibly on the passenger seat as long as the doors are locked.
options.b: They must be stored in the locked vehicle so that no one outside can directly infer the type or even the presence of the contents, and they must not remain unattended and freely accessible.
options.c: There is no longer any duty to secure them during a brief stop.
options.d: The weapon must always be taken into the cashier's booth when refueling.

waffen-aufbewahrung-09.explanation: The duty to secure weapons continues to apply even when a vehicle is briefly left unattended. Weapons and ammunition must be stored (e.g., in a locked, concealed trunk) so that no one outside can directly infer the type or even the presence of the contents, and so that unauthorized access is not possible.

waffen-aufbewahrung-10.question: During an extended vacation, may you informally hand your permit-required weapon over to an acquaintance for safekeeping if they have neither the corresponding weapons-law authorization nor a suitable container?

options.a: Yes, friends and acquaintances may keep weapons without any restriction.
options.b: Yes, as long as the acquaintance is an adult.
options.c: No, transferring the weapon to a person without the required weapons-law authorization or without a suitable security container is generally not permissible.
options.d: Yes, if the transfer is documented in writing.

waffen-aufbewahrung-10.explanation: Transferring a permit-required weapon generally requires that the recipient personally holds the necessary weapons-law authorization and can securely store the weapon in line with statutory requirements. Informally handing it to an unauthorized person without a suitable container is generally not permissible.

waffen-aufbewahrung-11.question: In what condition must weapons generally be kept in storage under the storage regulations?

options.a: Unloaded, in compliance with the respectively prescribed security precautions.
options.b: Loaded and ready to fire, so it can be used immediately in an emergency.
options.c: It does not matter whether the weapon is loaded.
options.d: Only the bolt/slide needs to be removed; it may otherwise remain loaded.

waffen-aufbewahrung-11.explanation: Under Sec. 13 AWaffV, weapons must be stored unloaded and in compliance with the respective security precautions. A weapon kept permanently loaded in storage does not meet the statutory requirements and significantly increases the risk of an unintentional discharge.

waffen-aufbewahrung-12.question: Do stricter special limits apply to storage in a not-permanently-inhabited building (e.g., a rarely used weekend house)?

options.a: No, exactly the same rules apply as in a continuously inhabited primary residence.
options.b: Yes, among other things a numerical cap applies to permit-required long guns, and storage is only permitted in a security container of a higher resistance grade.
options.c: No, storing permit-required weapons in a not-permanently-inhabited building is not allowed at all.
options.d: Yes, but only for ammunition, never for weapons.

waffen-aufbewahrung-12.explanation: Under Sec. 13(4) AWaffV, only up to a defined number of permit-required long guns may be stored in a not-permanently-inhabited building, and only in a security container of at least a higher resistance grade — a stricter departure from the general rules for a continuously inhabited home.

waffen-aufbewahrung-13.question: What does the transitional rule under weapons law regarding older VDMA 24992-standard security containers provide?

options.a: It bans continued use of such containers immediately and without exception.
options.b: It applies only to commercial weapons dealers, never to private individuals.
options.c: Under certain conditions, containers lawfully used for weapons storage before 6 July 2017 may continue to be used under the requirements that applied at that time (including under VDMA 24992-oriented rules).
options.d: It allows unlimited storage of any number of weapons regardless of container type.

waffen-aufbewahrung-13.explanation: Sec. 36(4) WaffG provides that current regulatory requirements do not apply if a security container was already lawfully used for weapons storage before 6 July 2017 and meets the requirements applicable at that time (including the prior version and old Sec. 13 AWaffV, partly oriented on VDMA 24992). This grandfathering rule is tied to narrow conditions.

waffen-handhabung-01.question: What basic rule applies when handling any firearm, regardless of whether it is loaded or not?

options.a: Only loaded weapons must be handled carefully; unloaded ones need no such care.
options.b: Every weapon should generally be treated as if it were loaded, including by constantly controlling the muzzle direction.
options.c: Weapons may be pointed at people in a private setting if one is certain they are unloaded.
options.d: Safety rules only apply at a shooting range, not while cleaning a weapon at home.

waffen-handhabung-01.explanation: A core rule of safe weapons handling is to treat every weapon as if it were loaded, regardless of its presumed state, including by constantly monitoring the muzzle direction so it never points at a person. This helps prevent accidents caused by mistaken assumptions.

waffen-handhabung-02.question: When is a firearm considered "ready to fire" under weapons law?

options.a: When it is loaded, i.e., ammunition or a projectile is positioned in the weapon such that a shot can be discharged directly by pulling the trigger.
options.b: Always, regardless of its actual loaded state.
options.c: Only if it is additionally unsafed and fitted with a telescopic sight.
options.d: Only for fully automatic weapons.

waffen-handhabung-02.explanation: A weapon is ready to fire when it is loaded — that is, ammunition is present in the weapon such that pulling the trigger will directly discharge a shot. This state must be clearly distinguished, both legally and for safety purposes, from an unloaded weapon.

waffen-handhabung-03.question: What basic safety steps should precede disassembling a weapon for cleaning or maintenance?

options.a: Visually looking at the weapon without opening it is sufficient.
options.b: The weapon should continue to be cleaned with the magazine inserted to save time.
options.c: The weapon must be unloaded (remove the magazine, check the chamber, and confirm it is empty) before disassembly begins.
options.d: Checking the chamber can be skipped once the magazine has been removed.

waffen-handhabung-03.explanation: Before any disassembly, cleaning, or maintenance, the weapon must be fully unloaded: remove the magazine and additionally check the chamber visually and/or by touch to confirm no round remains in it. Both steps are necessary, since removing the magazine alone does not rule out a chambered round.

waffen-handhabung-04.question: How does Sec. 32(2) of the German Criminal Code (StGB) define "Notwehr" (self-defense)?

options.a: Self-defense is any reaction to a situation perceived as unpleasant.
options.b: Self-defense is the defense that is necessary to avert a present, unlawful attack on oneself or another person.
options.c: Self-defense is exclusively defense against an attack that has already concluded.
options.d: Self-defense necessarily requires prior notification to an authority.

waffen-handhabung-04.explanation: Under Sec. 32(2) StGB, self-defense (Notwehr) is the defense that is necessary to avert a present, unlawful attack on oneself or another person. This definition is the basis for the criminal-law assessment of defensive acts, including those involving a firearm.

waffen-handhabung-05.question: What legal effect does a justified act of self-defense have under Sec. 32(1) StGB?

options.a: The act is not unlawful if it is warranted by self-defense.
options.b: The actor's culpability is excluded, but the act remains unlawful.
options.c: The act remains unlawful but is always punished more leniently.
options.d: Self-defense has no criminal-law significance at all.

waffen-handhabung-05.explanation: Sec. 32(1) StGB provides that a person who commits an act warranted by self-defense does not act unlawfully. Self-defense is thus a justification that removes the unlawfulness of the act entirely — not merely the culpability.

waffen-handhabung-06.question: Why is the principle of necessity (the least severe effective means) especially significant for using a firearm in a self-defense situation?

options.a: Because when using a firearm, no consideration of less severe means is required at all.
options.b: Because, given its potentially lethal effect, using a firearm is only covered by self-defense if no less severe, equally effective means is available to repel the attack.
options.c: Because necessity is only relevant if the attacker themself is using a firearm.
options.d: Because necessity depends solely on the severity of the attacker's prior convictions.

waffen-handhabung-06.explanation: Self-defense permits only the necessary defense, i.e., generally the least severe means suitable for immediately and reliably repelling the attack. Because of a firearm's potentially lethal effect, using one is only justified if no less drastic but equally effective means is available.

waffen-handhabung-07.question: How long does a self-defense situation under Sec. 32 StGB generally last?

options.a: Until the police arrive, regardless of the attacker's conduct.
options.b: As long as the unlawful attack is present, i.e., imminent, ongoing, or still continuing.
options.c: Indefinitely, even after the attacker has already fled.
options.d: Only for exactly one minute after the attack begins.

waffen-handhabung-07.explanation: Self-defense requires a "present" attack, meaning it must be imminent, currently occurring, or still ongoing. Once the attack has ended — for example because the attacker has fled — the self-defense situation ends; any "defense" after that point would no longer be self-defense but a separately assessed act.

waffen-handhabung-08.question: What is meant by "Putativnotwehr" (putative/apparent self-defense)?

options.a: A particularly far-reaching, statutorily permitted form of self-defense.
options.b: Defense of a third party (Nothilfe).
options.c: The mistaken belief that a self-defense situation exists, even though there is in fact no present, unlawful attack.
options.d: Deliberately provoking an attack in order to then be able to claim self-defense.

waffen-handhabung-08.explanation: "Putativnotwehr" describes a mistaken belief about the existence of a self-defense situation: the actor wrongly assumes they are being subjected to a present, unlawful attack, even though objectively no such attack exists. It is not genuine self-defense under Sec. 32 StGB but is assessed under the rules governing mistakes of fact.

waffen-handhabung-09.question: Is using a firearm to defend low-value property (e.g., an inexpensive item of little worth) covered by self-defense?

options.a: Yes, any property may be defended with any available means.
options.b: Generally not: where only the loss of a low-value item is at risk, using a firearm is typically not a defensive act warranted by self-defense.
options.c: Yes, but only if the attacker was warned beforehand.
options.d: This question has no practical relevance for the required expertise.

waffen-handhabung-09.explanation: Even though self-defense can formally apply to any legal interest, using a firearm given its potentially lethal effect is generally disproportionate — and therefore not "warranted" under Sec. 32 StGB — where only the loss of a low-value item is at stake.

waffen-handhabung-10.question: In a self-defense situation, should a warning be given before using a firearm, where possible?

options.a: No, a warning is never legally required or advisable.
options.b: Yes, to the extent circumstances allow, a warning should be given — for example by shouting or a warning shot — before using the weapon against a person.
options.c: No, a warning would eliminate the element of surprise and should therefore always be omitted.
options.d: A warning is only required when the attack involves bare fists.

waffen-handhabung-10.explanation: To the extent the specific circumstances allow, a warning should be given before using a firearm against an attacker — for example by shouting or firing a warning shot — to give the attacker a chance to abandon the attack. This reflects the principles of proportionality and necessity, though it is not an absolute requirement where circumstances leave no room for it.

waffen-handhabung-11.question: What is meant when a defensive act is assessed as "exceeding the limits of self-defense" (Notwehrexzess)?

options.a: The defensive act was lawful and exemplary in every respect.
options.b: The attacker had not actually attacked at all.
options.c: The limits of necessary defense were exceeded, for example by using a clearly excessive or no-longer-necessary means of defense relative to the actual attack.
options.d: The defense occurred even though no attack was yet imminent.

waffen-handhabung-11.explanation: "Exceeding self-defense" (Notwehrexzess) describes a situation where the actual defensive act goes beyond what was necessary to repel the attack — for instance, by using a disproportionately dangerous means against a clearly weaker attack. Unlike genuine self-defense, exceeding it is precisely not justified.

waffen-handhabung-12.question: What are the basic safety steps to follow when someone hands you a firearm or you take over a weapon from another person?

options.a: You should immediately check the loaded state yourself (check the magazine/cylinder, check the chamber), regardless of what the other person tells you.
options.b: A verbal assurance from the person handing it over that the weapon is unloaded is sufficient.
options.c: Muzzle direction does not matter during a handover as long as you trust the other person.
options.d: A check is only necessary for weapons you purchased yourself.

waffen-handhabung-12.explanation: Whenever taking over someone else's weapon, you must check its loaded state yourself, immediately — regardless of what the other person says — since misjudgments or miscommunication are among the most common causes of accidents in weapons handling. Muzzle direction must also be controlled continuously throughout the handover.
